paras: The killing of Margaret Auxier was the shooting death of a young woman by a party of men at her father's house near Yocum, Morgan County, Kentucky, in early March 1888. Several men were held on suspicion and lynching was talked of, and in August a man charged with the crime was himself found murdered after saying he would turn State's evidence.

According to a syndicated news column, a party of men rode up to the Auxier house on a Friday night and called to the father to come out. Instead he sent his daughter, who asked the men what they wanted, and they answered by firing on her at short range until her body was "literally riddled with bullets." The earliest report, a Kentucky dispatch of March 8, put the killing on "Tuesday afternoon," said her body had sixty-three bullet holes, and said she died pleading with the men not to shoot her any more. Neighbors could name no motive for the killing.

Four men were arrested soon afterward, and the dispatch added that other unknown parties had taken part. The syndicated column named those held on suspicion as Joseph S. Amos, David Lewis, and Noah and William Long, and said the only evidence against them was the father's statement that he thought he recognized one of the Lewises. The Stanford Semi-Weekly Interior Journal reported that "lynching is talked of," but no report of a lynching, indictment or trial was found.

The case surfaced again in August, when a Mount Sterling dispatch reported that Joe Lewis, "charged with the murder of Miss Auxier," had come home announcing he would turn State's evidence and then disappeared. His body was found with two bullet holes in the back of the head, dragged a hundred yards and thrown over a precipice 75 feet high. His cousins Dave and Al Lewis and a brother were charged and jailed at Mount Sterling, and the Louisville Weekly Courier-Journal wrote that a mob was talked of to take them out and hang them.

Only white papers covered the case, mostly in brief paragraphs within news-digest columns. Kentucky items called it a "cowardly murder" by a "cowardly crowd," and the same syndicated paragraph ran in the Maysville Evening Bulletin on March 14 and the Canton Stark County Democrat on March 15. No paper mentioned race in connection with the killing.

The August story traveled more widely, running from Washington to St. Paul under headlines such as "A Murderer Killed" and, in the New-York Tribune, "A Second Murder to Conceal the First." The Washington Evening Star's subhead held the crime "probably instigated by fear" that Lewis would turn state's evidence. Most versions described Lewis as charged with the Auxier murder, while the St. Paul Daily Globe called him "the murderer of Miss Auxier" and the Courier-Journal stated flatly that "Joe murdered Miss Auxier."

The reports disagree on the victim's name, which appears as Sallie Ohler, daughter of Zieh Ohler, only in the first dispatch and as Margaret Auxier everywhere else. They also differ on the day, Tuesday afternoon in that dispatch and Friday night in the syndicated column, and on who was held: the dispatch's OCR-damaged list reads "David Jeaeph, and Ames and Allred Lew!s," while the column named Amos, David Lewis and the two Longs. Joe Lewis, named in August as the man charged, appears in neither March list, and the Evening Star said he had evaded the officers at the time.

reader.title: Killing of Margaret Auxier
bases: A party of mounted men came to a family's house at night, called for the father and shot his daughter dead when she answered (A2, A3, A4); no accusation against her or lynching rationale is reported, and lynching was only 'talked of' afterward against the men held (A4).

A Kentucky dispatch (A1), the syndicated 'Pointed Paragraphs' item (A2, A3) and the Stanford Interior Journal (A4) independently agree that a young woman was shot to death at her father's house in Morgan County by several men and that men were held, though they differ on her name, the day and the names of the accused; the August reports (A5, A6, A11) refer back to the 'murder of Miss Auxier' as a known case.

Margaret Auxier, a young woman, daughter of a man named Auxier (A2, A3, A4); called Sallie Ohler, daughter of Zieh Ohler, in the Mar. 8 dispatch (A1). No paper states her race.

'A party of men' who rode up to the house (A2, A3); 'a cowardly crowd' (A4); four men arrested plus 'unknown parties' (A1). Their race is not stated.
